_note: Search metric co-movement patterns. Each maps a signature in the scorecard to a candidate mechanism and the cuts that would confirm or refute it. States are physical (up, down, flat, unknown), judged against each family's practical band: flat means the interval sits inside the band, unknown means it is too wide to tell. A cut with confirms_when/refutes_when is scored by script from evidence.json; others need an explicit outcome. 'reading' says whether a mechanism makes the movement good, bad, mixed or neutral news. Extend or override in the overlay (patterns.json); company metric names belong in the overlay's metric_families.json.

patterns.name: Better results, more satisfied clicks
patterns.mechanism: The ranking puts better results where users look, so more searches end in a satisfying click.

deep_dives.cut: success on triggered queries only (where the ranking actually changed) vs untriggered
deep_dives.confirms: a larger effect on triggered queries, diluted overall
deep_dives.refutes: the same effect on untouched queries, pointing to something other than ranking

deep_dives.cut: success by query class and device
deep_dives.confirms: the gain is largest where the change acts (for example tail queries for a recall change)
deep_dives.refutes: the gain is uniform, which a ranking change rarely produces

patterns.source: Kohavi, Tang, Xu 2020, ch. 20 (triggered analysis needs counterfactual logging, and the untriggered complement must look like an A/A)

patterns.name: More clicks, not more satisfaction
patterns.mechanism: Results look more clickable (titles, snippets or positions) but satisfy no more often, so CTR rises without long clicks.

deep_dives.cut: SAT clicks (dwell of 30 seconds or more) vs all clicks, by arm
deep_dives.confirms: clicks rise but SAT clicks don't
deep_dives.refutes: SAT clicks rise with clicks

deep_dives.cut: a similar query issued again within 5 minutes, by arm
deep_dives.confirms: quick re-queries rise after clicks
deep_dives.refutes: re-queries are flat

deep_dives.cut: config diff of presentation parameters (titles, snippets, thumbnails)
deep_dives.confirms: a presentation parameter differs between arms
deep_dives.refutes: only ranking differs (this doesn't rule it out: ranking can surface such results too)

deep_dives.cut: CTR and long-click rate by result position
deep_dives.confirms: the CTR gain sits in top positions and comes with short clicks
deep_dives.refutes: long clicks rise wherever CTR rises

deep_dives.cut: whole-page CTR vs CTR on the element that changed
deep_dives.confirms: element CTR rises while whole-page CTR is flat (clicks moved, not added)
deep_dives.refutes: whole-page CTR rises too

patterns.source: Hassan et al., CIKM 2013 (attractive snippets, SAT clicks at 30 s dwell); Dmitriev et al., A Dirty Dozen: Twelve Common Metric Interpretation Pitfalls, KDD 2017 (clicks shift between page elements)

patterns.name: More activity without more success
patterns.mechanism: Users click or search more while success doesn't rise. Published cases read this as attractive results, confusion or users struggling, not engagement, until a cut shows otherwise.
patterns.source: Kohavi et al., KDD 2012; Song, Shi, Fu, WWW 2013; Dmitriev et al., A Dirty Dozen, KDD 2017 (5.12, clicks up from confusion)

deep_dives.cut: success per query vs per user
deep_dives.confirms: success per query falls or holds while activity grows
deep_dives.refutes: success per query rises with activity

deep_dives.cut: a similar query issued again within 5 minutes, by arm
deep_dives.confirms: quick re-queries rise
deep_dives.refutes: re-queries are flat

deep_dives.cut: sessions per user vs queries per session, by arm
deep_dives.confirms: more queries inside the same sessions (retrying)
deep_dives.refutes: more sessions (coming back)

patterns.name: More searching because results got worse
patterns.mechanism: Users search more because they retry: reformulations rise and success doesn't, so higher query volume is a cost, not engagement. A worse ranker can raise queries and even sessions per user for days before engagement falls.

deep_dives.cut: success per query vs per user
deep_dives.confirms: success per query falls
deep_dives.refutes: success per query holds while volume grows

deep_dives.cut: a similar query issued again within 5 minutes, by arm
deep_dives.confirms: quick similar re-queries rise in treatment
deep_dives.refutes: re-queries are flat, so the extra queries are new needs

deep_dives.cut: navigational share of queries by arm, week by week
deep_dives.confirms: treatment users drift toward easy navigational queries (giving up on hard ones)
deep_dives.refutes: the query mix is stable

deep_dives.cut: reformulation rate by query class (head, torso, tail; navigational, informational)
deep_dives.confirms: reformulation rises on the classes the change touched
deep_dives.refutes: reformulation rises evenly, pointing to a logging or session change

deep_dives.cut: distribution of queries per session by arm
deep_dives.confirms: more long retry chains in treatment
deep_dives.refutes: more sessions, not longer ones

patterns.source: Kohavi et al., Five Puzzling Outcomes, KDD 2012 (a ranking bug raised queries per user 10% and revenue 30%); Song, Shi, Fu, WWW 2013 (a worse ranker raised sessions per user for days); Hassan et al., CIKM 2013 (re-query within 5 minutes)

patterns.name: More searching because search got better
patterns.mechanism: Users come back and search more because searches succeed more often. Treat it with suspicion: sessions per user rarely improves, and a short-lived rise can come from a worse ranker.

deep_dives.cut: sessions per user and return rate by arm
deep_dives.confirms: more return visits, not longer sessions
deep_dives.refutes: the extra queries sit inside the same sessions

deep_dives.cut: new vs returning users
deep_dives.confirms: the gain holds for returning users
deep_dives.refutes: the gain is only in first-week users (novelty)

patterns.source: Kohavi, 2017 talk (sessions per user improves in about 1 in 5000 Bing experiments); Song, Shi, Fu, WWW 2013

patterns.name: Slower results cost engagement
patterns.mechanism: The treatment serves results more slowly, and slower pages lose clicks and raise abandonment, which can hide a relevance gain. Speed effects tend to grow over weeks rather than fade.

deep_dives.cut: abandonment and CTR by latency bucket, per arm
deep_dives.confirms: the loss sits in the slow buckets
deep_dives.refutes: the loss is flat across latency buckets

deep_dives.cut: latency by page type and load type (cached reloads vs fresh loads), by arm
deep_dives.confirms: latency rises on the same page types
deep_dives.refutes: the page mix changed, so latency moved without pages getting slower

deep_dives.cut: effect by device and network type
deep_dives.confirms: mobile or slow networks carry the loss
deep_dives.refutes: the loss is the same everywhere

deep_dives.cut: relevance metrics on queries where latency didn't change
deep_dives.confirms: relevance improves once latency is held fixed
deep_dives.refutes: no gain even at equal latency

patterns.source: Brutlag, Google, 2009 (400 ms delay: -0.44% searches in weeks 1-3, -0.76% in weeks 4-6, still -0.21% after removal); Dmitriev et al., A Dirty Dozen: Twelve Common Metric Interpretation Pitfalls, KDD 2017 (latency moved by page mix)

patterns.name: More results for hard queries, lower precision
patterns.mechanism: The change returns results for queries that used to get none, but those results are weak, so averages over all queries fall.

deep_dives.cut: success and CTR on queries that had zero results in control
deep_dives.confirms: these queries now get results but low success
deep_dives.refutes: they succeed at the normal rate

deep_dives.cut: the same metrics excluding those queries
deep_dives.confirms: the rest of the traffic is flat
deep_dives.refutes: the drop is broad

patterns.source: Dmitriev et al., A Dirty Dozen: Twelve Common Metric Interpretation Pitfalls, KDD 2017 (ratio metrics move with their denominator); reasoned, no published case of this exact signature

patterns.name: Answers on the page reduce clicks
patterns.mechanism: More users get their answer from the results page itself (answers, richer snippets), so they leave without clicking and don't retry.

deep_dives.cut: abandonment on queries with an answer or rich snippet vs without
deep_dives.confirms: the rise sits on answer-bearing queries
deep_dives.refutes: the rise sits on queries without an answer

deep_dives.cut: a similar query issued again within 5 minutes after an abandoned query
deep_dives.confirms: abandoned users don't come back to retry
deep_dives.refutes: abandoned users retry

deep_dives.cut: config diff of presentation parameters (answers, rich snippets)
deep_dives.confirms: an answer or snippet parameter differs between arms
deep_dives.refutes: only ranking differs (this doesn't rule it out: ranking can surface such results too)

deep_dives.cut: abandonment by device
deep_dives.confirms: the rise is larger on mobile, where good abandonment is common
deep_dives.refutes: the rise is the same on desktop

patterns.source: Li, Huffman, Tokuda, SIGIR 2009 (good abandonment, higher on mobile); Pew Research 2025 (clicks 8% vs 15% with AI summaries)

patterns.name: Worse results make users give up
patterns.mechanism: Users leave without clicking because results got worse, not because the answer was on the page.
patterns.source: Li, Huffman, Tokuda, SIGIR 2009 (good vs bad abandonment); Song, Shi, Fu, WWW 2013

deep_dives.cut: abandonment on queries with an answer or rich snippet vs without
deep_dives.confirms: the rise sits on queries without an answer
deep_dives.refutes: the rise sits on answer-bearing queries

deep_dives.cut: config diff of presentation parameters (answers, rich snippets)
deep_dives.confirms: only ranking differs
deep_dives.refutes: an answer or snippet parameter differs

patterns.name: Some queries win, others lose
patterns.mechanism: The change helps many queries and hurts others, so averages hide both: more clicks overall while a slice of queries is abandoned more.

deep_dives.cut: per-query win/loss: share of queries whose success rose vs fell
deep_dives.confirms: a sizeable group of losing queries
deep_dives.refutes: losses are spread thinly, not concentrated

deep_dives.cut: abandonment by query class and query length
deep_dives.confirms: the abandonment rise sits in one class
deep_dives.refutes: abandonment rises evenly

patterns.source: Dmitriev et al., A Dirty Dozen: Twelve Common Metric Interpretation Pitfalls, KDD 2017 (heterogeneous effects); reasoned from averages hiding opposite effects

patterns.name: Organic results take attention from ads
patterns.mechanism: Better organic results draw clicks that used to go to ads, so ad clicks fall while organic engagement rises.

deep_dives.cut: ad clicks by ad position and by the rank of the first satisfying organic result
deep_dives.confirms: ad clicks fall most where a good organic result now sits above the ad
deep_dives.refutes: ad clicks fall evenly

deep_dives.cut: ad impressions per query and revenue per user
deep_dives.confirms: impressions hold and clicks fall
deep_dives.refutes: fewer ads are shown (an ad-serving change)

patterns.source: Dmitriev et al., A Dirty Dozen: Twelve Common Metric Interpretation Pitfalls, KDD 2017 (ad load by page type); Kohavi et al. 2012 (bad organic results raise revenue)

patterns.name: Worse organic results make ads look better
patterns.mechanism: Revenue or ad clicks rise because organic results got worse: users search more and ads look relatively more relevant. Bing saw a ranking bug raise revenue per user 30%.
patterns.source: Kohavi et al., Five Puzzling Outcomes, KDD 2012

deep_dives.cut: success per query vs per user
deep_dives.confirms: success per query falls
deep_dives.refutes: success per query holds

deep_dives.cut: ad clicks per query vs organic clicks per query, by arm
deep_dives.confirms: ad clicks rise where organic clicks fall
deep_dives.refutes: both rise together

patterns.name: A ratio moved because its denominator moved
patterns.mechanism: {ratio} moved because {denominator} moved ({denominator_change}), not because {numerator} changed; the ratio's story is about volume, not quality.

deep_dives.cut: {numerator} and {denominator} per user, side by side
deep_dives.confirms: the denominator carries the change
deep_dives.refutes: the numerator moves too

deep_dives.cut: what changed the {denominator} (query volume, sessions, logging of searches)
deep_dives.confirms: a volume or logging change explains it
deep_dives.refutes: volume is steady

deep_dives.cut: the same clicks over the finest denominator that doesn't move itself (for example clicks per session)
deep_dives.confirms: the effect disappears on a stable denominator
deep_dives.refutes: the effect holds on a stable denominator

patterns.source: Dmitriev et al., A Dirty Dozen: Twelve Common Metric Interpretation Pitfalls, KDD 2017 (module CTR -40% while clicks +74% and impressions +200%)

patterns.name: The effect sits in one segment
patterns.mechanism: {metric}'s change comes mostly from {segment} ({share} of the overall change), and segments differ more than noise allows.

deep_dives.cut: {metric} for {segment} vs the rest, with triggered queries only
deep_dives.confirms: the change is real and confined to {segment}
deep_dives.refutes: the other segments move too once diluted traffic is removed

deep_dives.cut: what the treatment changes for {segment} (ranking features, coverage, rendering)
deep_dives.confirms: a mechanism specific to {segment}
deep_dives.refutes: nothing in the change targets {segment}

deep_dives.cut: sample split and event logging within {segment}, by arm
deep_dives.confirms: the segment is balanced and logs the same way
deep_dives.refutes: the segment itself is imbalanced or logs differently (an artifact)

patterns.source: Dmitriev et al., A Dirty Dozen: Twelve Common Metric Interpretation Pitfalls, KDD 2017 (effects confined to a country, browser or version); tail-query lifts reported for semantic retrieval (snippet-level)

patterns.name: The effect is fading
patterns.mechanism: The effect shrinks with each day users have had the treatment, so the long-run effect is likely smaller than the average. UI changes tend to fade; ranking, speed and ad-load effects tend to grow, so a fading ranking effect deserves a second look.

deep_dives.cut: effect by days since first exposure, per weekly cohort
deep_dives.confirms: every cohort fades the same way
deep_dives.refutes: late cohorts start lower (cohort mix, not novelty)

deep_dives.cut: new vs returning users
deep_dives.confirms: returning users fade
deep_dives.refutes: only new users differ

patterns.source: Song, Shi, Fu, WWW 2013; Brutlag 2009; Hohnhold, O'Brien, Tang, KDD 2015 (ads blindness grows over months)

patterns.name: A data or logging problem, not user behaviour
patterns.mechanism: A validity check flagged the data itself, so the movements may reflect logging, assignment or export problems rather than users.

deep_dives.cut: event counts per user by arm for every logged event the change could touch
deep_dives.confirms: one arm logs differently
deep_dives.refutes: logging is identical

deep_dives.cut: exposure counts by day, platform and browser
deep_dives.confirms: the imbalance sits in one slice
deep_dives.refutes: the imbalance is everywhere (assignment problem)

deep_dives.cut: client-logged vs server-logged versions of the same metric, by arm
deep_dives.confirms: only client events move (telemetry loss differs by arm)
deep_dives.refutes: client and server agree

deep_dives.cut: share of users removed by bot and spam filters, by arm
deep_dives.confirms: filters remove different shares in each arm
deep_dives.refutes: filter rates match

patterns.source: Dmitriev et al., A Dirty Dozen: Twelve Common Metric Interpretation Pitfalls, KDD 2017 (telemetry loss in one arm, bot filters hitting engaged users, metric-level sample ratio mismatch)
